content: I am a PhD student with the NetSyn lab at Princeton University, where I research network security and its intersection with decentralized consensus.

HotNets '26 The 25th ACM Workshop on Hot Topics in Networks · Salt Lake City, UT
Constantine Doumanidis, Hongyu Hè, Maria Apostolaki
NetSyn · Princeton University
Paper (PDF) Interactive demo Talk Cite In short # Problem LLM agents still struggle to find the root cause of network faults. At the same time network operator traces contain knowledge that would help diagnosis, but no available dataset captures this process.
Insight Students in networking courses break and fix real-looking networks every semester. We can extract realistic, labeled and shareable debugging traces from their terminal sessions.
Challenges Deciding what to log, at what granularity, and then extracting clean meaningful diagnostic trajectories from noisy, concurrent student terminal sessions.
We can automatically mine meaningful action traces from networking courses. Mined faults are challenging benchmarks for root cause analysis (RCA) agents. Runbooks generated from mined patterns effectively guide RCA agents. Abstract # Network operators diagnose faults by issuing commands, forming hypotheses, and iterating to a fix. Yet, no dataset captures this diagnostic process. Production traces are locked down, and synthetic benchmarks reduce debugging to single injected faults on homogeneous topologies. We propose mining students’ actions during the completion of networking course assignments as a source of realistic, labeled, and shareable debugging traces. We test this idea in the mini-Internet, an open-source platform in which students configure their part of a miniature of the Internet, naturally generating cascading, multi-protocol failures and the trajectories that fix them. Realizing this opportunity requires confronting two challenges: what to log and at what granularity, and how to extract clean diagnostic trajectories from noisy, concurrent student sessions. We describe our initial design and the open research problems ahead. Our preliminary results show that non-trivial faults such as misconfigurations and diagnostic patterns can be mined from student logs automatically, and that the resulting guidance improves the root cause analysis accuracy of LLM agents.
Talk # Results # We mined two example misconfigurations from student traces, an L2 subnetting fault (overlapping subnets, dropped packets) and a BGP traffic engineering fault (bad AS-path prepending, high latency), and gave them to LLM root cause analysis agents. Without help, the mined faults are hard: GPT-5.4 mini never finds the BGP root cause, and GPT-5.5 finds the L2 root cause in 1 of 5 runs. With runbooks generated automatically from the mined patterns, both models find the root cause in every run, in most settings with fewer tokens: GPT-5.5 on the BGP fault drops from 239k to 34k tokens per run.
Without runbooks With runbooks RCA success rate Tokens per run (input + output, mean) 5 runs per setting. From Table 5 of the paper.
Try it yourself # Play the student in our guided demo, recorded on a real lab network: watch a fault get diagnosed and fixed in the terminals, see which troubleshooting pattern the commands match, and compare the run with AI agents, with and without runbooks. No account needed.

content: Financial Cryptography & Data Security 2026 Paper PDF # FC'26 Pre-proceedings Abstract # With the promise of greater decentralization and sustainability, Ethereum transitioned from a Proof-of-Work (PoW) to a Proof-of-Stake (PoS) consensus mechanism. The new consensus protocol introduces novel vulnerabilities that warrant further investigation. The goal of this paper is to investigate the security of Ethereum’s PoS system from an Internet routing perspective. To this end, this paper makes two contributions: First, we devise a novel framework for inferring the distribution of validators on the Internet without disturbing the real network. Second, we introduce a class of network-level attacks on Ethereum’s PoS system that jointly exploit Internet routing vulnerabilities with the protocol’s reward and penalty mechanisms. We describe two representative attacks: StakeBleed, where the attacker triggers an inactivity leak, halting block finality and causing financial losses for all validators; and KnockBlock, where the attacker increases her expected MEV gains by preventing targeted blocks from being included in the chain. We find that both attacks are practical and effective. An attacker executing StakeBleed can inflict losses of almost 300 ETH in just 2 hours by hijacking as few as 30 IP prefixes. An attacker implementing KnockBlock could increase their MEV expected gains by 44.5% while hijacking a single prefix for less than 2 minutes. Our paper serves as a call to action for validators to reinforce their Internet routing infrastructure and for the Ethereum P2P protocol to implement stronger mechanisms to conceal validator locations.
title: Routing Attacks in Ethereum PoS: A Systematic Exploration
